# ISO 27001 Gap Analysis Checklist

## Context and assumptions

You're a 250-person SaaS company, AWS-hosted, serving EU and US customers, mid-flight on SOC 2 Type II, with ITIL-based change, incident, and configuration management already running. That gives you a meaningful head start. SOC 2 Trust Services Criteria overlap roughly 60–70% with ISO 27001 Annex A, and your ITIL processes will produce much of the documentary evidence auditors expect. The biggest gaps will likely be in formal ISMS governance (Clauses 4–10), complete asset inventory, supplier security, and business continuity testing.

I've organized everything into three priority tiers: foundational work that must come first, core controls where you likely have partial coverage, and advanced or specialized controls you can tackle last. Within each tier, items are roughly ordered by dependency and audit impact.

---

## Tier 1 — Foundational (do first, months 1–3)

These are the mandatory ISMS clauses (4–10) plus the Annex A controls that underpin everything else. Without these, a Stage 1 auditor will stop the process.

**1.1 — Establish the ISMS scope and context (Clauses 4.1–4.3)**

Define your organizational context, interested parties (EU customers, US customers, regulators, staff), and ISMS boundaries. For a SaaS provider your scope will likely be "the design, development, delivery, and support of [product] hosted on AWS, including all supporting infrastructure, people, and processes." Document this in a one- to two-page scope statement. Your SOC 2 scoping work is directly reusable here.

ITIL coverage: None directly, but your service catalogue and configuration management system (CMS) will help define the boundary.

Quick win: Reuse your SOC 2 system description as the starting point.

**1.2 — Leadership commitment and roles (Clauses 5.1–5.3)**

You need documented executive commitment (a signed information security policy), a named ISMS owner (typically the CISO or head of security), and defined roles and responsibilities. The policy must be communicated to all employees.

Annex A: 5.1 (Policies for information security), 5.2 (Information security roles and responsibilities).

ITIL coverage: ITIL's organizational structure helps but doesn't produce the ISO-required policy or role assignments.

Quick win: Draft and sign the top-level information security policy — it can be two pages. Assign ISMS ownership formally.

**1.3 — Risk assessment and treatment (Clause 6.1.2, 6.1.3)**

This is the engine of the ISMS. You need a documented risk assessment methodology (likelihood × impact is fine), a risk register, defined risk acceptance criteria approved by management, and a risk treatment plan that maps each unacceptable risk to Annex A controls. The output feeds directly into the Statement of Applicability.

Annex A: 5.7 (Threat intelligence — feeds risk identification).

ITIL coverage: ITIL's risk management practice provides a process skeleton, but you need a formal, security-specific risk register.

Quick win: If your SOC 2 readiness included a risk assessment, adapt it. Add likelihood/impact scoring and map findings to Annex A controls.

**1.4 — Statement of Applicability (SoA)**

A mandatory document listing all 93 Annex A controls, stating whether each is applicable or not (with justification for exclusions), and noting implementation status. This is the single most important audit artifact.

Quick win: Start with a spreadsheet of all 93 controls, pre-populate "implemented" for controls your ITIL processes and SOC 2 work already cover, and mark gaps.

**1.5 — Asset inventory completion (Annex A 5.9, 5.10, 5.11, 5.12, 5.13)**

You flagged this as partial. The auditor will want a complete inventory of information assets (data stores, databases, S3 buckets), supporting assets (servers, SaaS tools, endpoints, network devices), software assets, and people/roles with classified ownership, classification labels (e.g., Public / Internal / Confidential / Restricted), and acceptable use rules. Controls 5.10 (acceptable use), 5.12 (classification), and 5.13 (labelling) all depend on a finished inventory.

ITIL coverage: Your configuration management practice and CMS should already track CIs. Extend it to cover data assets and apply classification.

Quick win: Export your AWS resource inventory (AWS Config, AWS Organizations), merge with your CMS, and add ownership and classification columns. This can close the gap fast.

**1.6 — Documented information and document control (Clauses 7.5, Annex A 5.1, 5.37)**

ISO 27001 requires controlled documents with version history, approval, and distribution. You need a document control procedure and a central repository.

ITIL coverage: ITIL's knowledge management practice covers some of this.

Quick win: If you use Confluence, SharePoint, or similar, create an ISMS space with a naming convention, version control, and an approval workflow. Many orgs overthink this.

---

## Tier 2 — Core controls (months 2–5, many already partially covered)

These are the Annex A controls most relevant to a SaaS company on AWS with ITIL processes. I've grouped them by theme and flagged where your existing processes likely give you coverage.

**2.1 — People security (Annex A 6.1–6.8)**

| Control | Description | ITIL coverage | Likely status | Action needed |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 6.1 Screening | Background checks before employment | None | Partial (check HR) | Formalize screening policy, ensure it covers contractors |
| 6.2 Terms and conditions | Security obligations in contracts | None | Likely in place | Verify employment contracts include confidentiality and security clauses |
| 6.3 Awareness and training | Security awareness program | Workforce and talent mgmt | Partial if SOC 2 required it | Implement annual training with tracked completion; add role-specific training for devs |
| 6.4 Disciplinary process | Consequences for violations | None | Likely in HR policy | Document and reference in security policy |
| 6.5 After termination | Obligations survive departure | None | Check contracts | Ensure NDAs and IP clauses survive termination |
| 6.6 Confidentiality agreements | NDAs | None | Likely partial | Extend to contractors and third parties |
| 6.7 Remote working | Security for remote work | None | Likely informal | Document remote work security requirements (VPN, endpoint, screen lock) |
| 6.8 Security event reporting | Staff report incidents | Incident management | Covered if incident process includes reporting channel | Ensure all staff know how to report; test annually |

Quick win: If SOC 2 required security awareness training, you already have it — just document the program and ensure completion records exist.

**2.2 — Access control (Annex A 5.15–5.18, 8.2–8.5)**

| Control | Description | ITIL coverage | Likely status | Action needed |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 5.15 Access control policy | Documented policy | Access management | Likely informal | Write a one-page access control policy (need-to-know, least privilege) |
| 5.16 Identity management | Unique IDs, lifecycle | Access management | Likely via IdP (Okta, Azure AD) | Document identity lifecycle (joiner/mover/leaver) |
| 5.17 Authentication | MFA, password policy | Access management | Likely in place for SOC 2 | Verify MFA on all production, admin, and SaaS accounts |
| 5.18 Access rights | Provisioning and review | Access management | Likely partial | Implement quarterly access reviews with evidence |
| 8.2 Privileged access | Admin account controls | Access management | Likely partial | Document privileged access procedure, enforce just-in-time or break-glass |
| 8.3 Information access restriction | App-level controls | None | Likely in product | Document RBAC model in application |
| 8.5 Secure authentication | Hardened auth mechanisms | None | Likely in place | Verify password hashing, session management, brute-force protection |

Quick win: If you use an IdP with SSO and MFA, your evidence is largely in the IdP's logs and config. Export and document.

**2.3 — Change, incident, and configuration management (Annex A 5.24–5.28, 8.9, 8.32, 8.33)**

This is where your ITIL maturity pays off.

| Control | Description | ITIL coverage | Likely status | Action needed |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 8.32 Change management | Controlled changes | Change enablement | **Covered** | Map ITIL change process to this control in SoA; ensure security review is a gate |
| 8.9 Configuration management | Secure baselines | Service config mgmt | **Covered** | Document baseline configs for AWS (use AWS Config rules or CIS benchmarks) |
| 5.24 Incident mgmt planning | Process exists | Incident management | **Covered** | Verify process includes security-specific classification and escalation |
| 5.25 Assessment and decision | Classify severity | Incident management | **Covered** | Ensure classification criteria distinguish security incidents |
| 5.26 Response to incidents | Containment, eradication | Incident management | **Mostly covered** | Add forensic preservation and communication steps |
| 5.27 Learning from incidents | Post-incident review | Problem management | Likely in place | Ensure PIRs are documented and feed back into risk register |
| 5.28 Evidence collection | Chain of custody | None | Likely gap | Write a short evidence collection procedure (log preservation, timestamps, chain of custody) |
| 8.33 Test information | Protect test data | None | Unknown | Ensure production data is anonymized/masked in non-prod environments |

Quick win: Your ITIL change and incident processes probably need only light annotation ("this process satisfies Annex A 8.32") and a security gate added to the change workflow.

**2.4 — Cryptography, network, and infrastructure security (Annex A 8.24, 8.20–8.23, 8.26, 8.7, 8.1, 8.8)**

| Control | Description | Likely status (AWS SaaS) | Action needed |
|---|---|---|---|
| 8.24 Use of cryptography | TLS, encryption at rest | Likely in place (ACM, KMS, RDS encryption) | Document cryptographic standards (algorithms, key lengths, key management via KMS) |
| 8.20 Network security | VPC segmentation, security groups | Likely in place | Document network architecture diagram with security controls |
| 8.21 Security of network services | Managed services, WAF | Likely partial | Verify WAF, DDoS protection (Shield), and document |
| 8.22 Segregation of networks | Prod/dev/staging separation | Likely in place | Document VPC/account separation; verify no prod-to-dev bridging |
| 8.23 Web filtering | Outbound filtering | May be a gap | Assess need; can use DNS filtering or proxy for corporate endpoints |
| 8.26 Application security requirements | Secure SDLC | Likely partial (SOC 2 often requires this) | Document SDLC with security gates (threat modelling, code review, SAST/DAST) |
| 8.7 Malware protection | Endpoint and server AV/EDR | Likely in place | Verify EDR on all endpoints and document |
| 8.1 User endpoint devices | Device management | Likely partial | Formalize MDM or endpoint policy (encryption, screen lock, patching) |
| 8.8 Vulnerability management | Scanning and patching | Likely in place for SOC 2 | Document scan cadence, SLAs for remediation by severity, and evidence |

Quick win: Most of these are AWS-native. Export your AWS Config compliance dashboard, Security Hub findings, and KMS key policies as evidence.

**2.5 — Logging and monitoring (Annex A 8.15, 8.16, 8.17)**

| Control | Description | Likely status | Action needed |
|---|---|---|---|
| 8.15 Logging | Audit trails for access, changes, errors | Likely in place (CloudTrail, application logs) | Document what is logged, retention periods (align with legal/contractual), and tamper protection |
| 8.16 Monitoring activities | SIEM or alerting | Likely partial | Ensure alerts for security-relevant events (failed logins, privilege escalation, config changes); document monitoring procedures |
| 8.17 Clock synchronization | NTP across systems | Covered by AWS | Document; trivial for cloud |

Quick win: If you have CloudTrail, VPC Flow Logs, and GuardDuty enabled, document and reference them.

**2.6 — Backup and continuity (Annex A 8.13, 8.14, 5.29, 5.30)**

| Control | Description | Likely status | Action needed |
|---|---|---|---|
| 8.13 Information backup | Backup policy and testing | Likely in place (RDS snapshots, S3 versioning) | Document backup schedule, retention, and **test restores** quarterly with evidence |
| 8.14 Redundancy | HA design | Likely in place (multi-AZ) | Document architecture and failover procedures |
| 5.29 Disruption planning | Business continuity | May be a gap | Write a business continuity plan covering key scenarios (AWS region failure, key person loss, ransomware) |
| 5.30 ICT readiness for business continuity | DR testing | Likely partial | Conduct and document a DR test; define RTO/RPO per service tier |

Quick win: If you already have multi-AZ and automated snapshots, document them and run one verified restore test.

---

## Tier 3 — Specialized and advanced (months 4–6+)

**3.1 — Supplier and third-party security (Annex A 5.19–5.23)**

Critical for a SaaS company using AWS and likely dozens of sub-processors.

| Control | Action needed |
|---|---|
| 5.19 Supplier security policy | Write a supplier security management policy |
| 5.20 Addressing security in supplier agreements | Ensure contracts include security clauses, audit rights, breach notification |
| 5.21 Managing security in the ICT supply chain | Assess supply chain risk (AWS, CI/CD tools, monitoring SaaS) |
| 5.22 Monitoring and review of supplier services | Implement annual supplier reviews (collect SOC 2 reports, ISO certs) |
| 5.23 Cloud service security | Document AWS shared responsibility model, your responsibilities, and how you verify AWS controls |

Quick win: Collect SOC 2/ISO 27001 reports from your top 10 suppliers now. Many (AWS, Datadog, PagerDuty, etc.) publish them. Create a supplier register with risk ratings.

**3.2 — Privacy and data protection (Annex A 5.34, 5.35, 5.36)**

With EU customers you're subject to GDPR, so these controls are non-negotiable.

| Control | Action needed |
|---|---|
| 5.34 Privacy and PII protection | Document how you identify and protect PII; align with GDPR obligations |
| 5.35 Independent review | Plan for internal audit or external review of the ISMS (Clause 9.2 requirement too) |
| 5.36 Compliance with policies and standards | Implement compliance checking (can be part of internal audit) |

Quick win: If you have a GDPR data processing agreement template and a data processing register, reference them.

**3.3 — Physical security (Annex A 7.1–7.14)**

Since production is on AWS, most physical controls apply only to your offices. The auditor will verify that AWS's physical controls are addressed via the shared responsibility model and AWS's own ISO 27001 certificate.

For offices: ensure visitor logs, clean desk policy, secure disposal of media, and physical access controls to server rooms (if any) are documented. This is usually low effort.

**3.4 — Secure development (Annex A 8.25–8.31, 8.33, 8.34)**

| Control | Action needed |
|---|---|

> **[Company Name] — Information Security Policy**
>
> **Version:** 1.0 | **Classification:** Internal | **Owner:** [CISO Name] | **Approved by:** [CEO Name] | **Date:** [Date] | **Review:** Annual
>
> ---
>
> **Purpose**
>
> This policy establishes management's direction and commitment to protecting the confidentiality, integrity, and availability of information entrusted to [Company Name] by its customers, employees, and partners.
>
> **Scope**
>
> This policy applies to all employees, contractors, and third parties who access [Company Name] information, systems, or facilities. It covers all information assets within the ISMS scope as defined in the ISMS Scope Statement.
>
> **Principles**
>
> [Company Name] commits to the following principles. First, we will protect customer data and company information commensurate with its sensitivity and value, applying controls proportionate to assessed risk. Second, we will comply with all applicable legal, regulatory, and contractual obligations, including the EU General Data Protection Regulation and customer contractual commitments. Third, we will manage information security risk through a systematic process of identification, assessment, treatment, and ongoing monitoring, documented in our risk register and Statement of Applicability. Fourth, we will grant access to information and systems on a need-to-know and least-privilege basis, verifying identity through strong authentication. Fifth, we will prepare for, detect, respond to, and recover from information security incidents in a timely manner, learning from each event to improve our defences. Sixth, we will foster a culture of security awareness through regular training and clear communication of responsibilities. Seventh, we will continually improve the effectiveness of our Information Security Management System through internal audit, management review, corrective action, and measurement against defined objectives.
>
> **Responsibilities**
>
> The Chief Executive Officer bears overall accountability for information security. The [CISO / Head of Security] is responsible for maintaining the ISMS, conducting risk assessments, reporting to senior management, and coordinating security activities. All managers are responsible for ensuring their teams understand and comply with this policy and supporting policies. All employees and contractors are responsible for complying with security policies, completing required training, and reporting security events promptly.
>
> **Information security objectives**
>
> Management will define measurable information security objectives annually, aligned with business strategy and risk appetite, and will review progress during management reviews. > This policy is supported by topic-specific policies and procedures covering access control, acceptable use, data classification, incident management, supplier security, cryptography, secure development, business continuity, and other domains as required by our Statement of Applicability. > **Enforcement**

> Violations of this policy or its supporting policies may result in disciplinary action up to and including termination of employment or contract, and may also result in legal action where applicable.
>
> **Review**

> This policy is reviewed at least annually and updated whenever significant changes occur to the organisation, its risk environment, or applicable regulations. All changes require approval by the CEO or delegated authority.
